description: Religious teachings on wealth, poverty, fair pay, excessive interest, people-trafficking and the role of charity.
content_html:
Religious Attitudes to Wealth

Religious traditions do not uniformly condemn wealth. Most teach that wealth in itself is morally neutral — what matters is how it is acquired, held and used. The concept of stewardship in Christianity holds that everything humans possess ultimately belongs to God, and that humans are responsible for managing these resources on God’s behalf. Genesis 1:28 describes God giving humanity dominion over creation; many Christian theologians interpret this as a duty of care and responsible management, not unlimited exploitation. The Acts of the Apostles (2:44–45) describes the earliest Christian community sharing their possessions: “All the believers were together and had everything in common. They sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need.”

Jesus taught extensively about wealth and poverty. His parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16–21) warns against hoarding wealth without concern for others. The story of Zacchaeus (Luke 19) presents a wealthy tax collector who, on meeting Jesus, gives half his possessions to the poor and repays those he has cheated fourfold — illustrating the transformation that Jesus’s teaching was expected to produce. Catholic Social Teaching, developed through Rerum Novarum (1891) and continued in Laudato Si’ (2015), affirms the right to private property while insisting that wealth carries social obligations and that the needs of the poorest must be met.

Key Fact

Five religious giving duties: Zakat (Islam — obligatory giving, one of the Five Pillars, 2.5% of savings above a threshold); Tzedakah (Judaism — righteous giving or charity, understood as a duty rather than an optional gift); Dasvandh (Sikhism — tithing one tenth of income, contributing to langar and gurdwara community work); Dana (Buddhism — generosity as the first perfection, given to the sangha or those in need); Stewardship (Christianity — using all resources wisely as God’s caretakers, expressed through giving to the poor and tithing).

Islamic Teaching on Wealth and Poverty

Zakat is the third Pillar of Islam: every Muslim who possesses savings above a minimum threshold (the nisab) for a full lunar year must give 2.5% of that wealth to those in need. Zakat is understood not as optional charity but as a religious duty, purifying the remainder of one’s wealth and redistributing resources across the ummah. The Quran states: “And establish prayer and give zakat, and whatever good you put forward for yourselves — you will find it with Allah” (Quran 2:110, paraphrase). In addition to zakat, Muslims are encouraged to give sadaqah (voluntary charitable giving) freely and without expectation of return.

Islamic teaching strictly prohibits riba — the charging of interest or usury. The Quran explicitly forbids riba (Quran 2:275), stating that those who consume interest will arise on the Day of Judgement as those who have been touched by Satan. This prohibition is grounded in the belief that charging interest exploits those in financial difficulty and concentrates wealth unjustly. Islamic finance today operates through structures such as profit-sharing agreements (mudarabah) and leasing arrangements (ijara) that comply with this prohibition. There is debate within Islamic scholarship about the precise definition of riba and how it applies in modern financial systems — with different Sunni and Shi’a scholarly opinions on specific modern financial products.

Tzedakah is the Jewish practice of charitable giving. Crucially, the Hebrew word tzedakah is related to tzedek (justice or righteousness): giving to those in need is understood not as optional generosity but as a matter of justice, because the world’s resources belong ultimately to God and must be shared equitably. The twelfth-century Jewish philosopher Maimonides described a “ladder of tzedakah” ranking different forms of giving from lowest (giving reluctantly and less than one should) to highest (giving someone the means to support themselves independently). The concept of the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25) — in which debts were cancelled and land returned to its original owners — grounds the Jewish tradition’s concern that accumulated wealth should not permanently disadvantage the poor.

Exploitation, Fair Pay and People-Trafficking

Religious teachings on wealth carry specific implications for how wealth is acquired, not just how it is given away. The concept of unfair pay is condemned across traditions. Catholic Social Teaching, drawing on Rerum Novarum (1891), explicitly stated that workers have a right to a wage sufficient to support themselves and their families in dignity. Gaudium et Spes (1965) affirmed the right of all workers to just and equitable remuneration. The Hebrew Bible repeatedly commands fair treatment of workers: “Do not take advantage of a hired worker who is poor and needy... Pay them their wages each day before sunset” (Deuteronomy 24:14–15). Sikh teaching condemns exploitation through the principle of honest living (kirat karna — earning one’s livelihood through honest work).

People-trafficking is among the most serious forms of exploitation condemned by religious traditions. It treats human beings as commodities and strips them of freedom, dignity and autonomy. Christian organisations including the Salvation Army and the Catholic Church’s Caritas network have been active in anti-trafficking work in Britain and globally. Islamic teaching grounds opposition to people-trafficking in the principle of human dignity (karama) and the prohibition on enslaving free people. Jewish teaching grounds it in Pikuach Nefesh — the duty to save human life — and in the memory of the Exodus from slavery in Egypt, which is central to Jewish identity.

Buddhist teaching holds that attachment to wealth is one of the causes of suffering (dukkha). The Three Poisons include greed (lobha) as a root cause of unsatisfactory living. The Buddha taught the Middle Way — avoiding both extreme asceticism and excessive indulgence — and monks in the Theravada tradition own very little, relying on the lay community for material support through dana (giving). Lay Buddhists are encouraged to give generously, to avoid livelihoods that involve harming others (covered in the Right Livelihood limb of the Eightfold Path), and to hold wealth without clinging to it.

Sikh teaching describes dasvandh — the giving of one tenth of one’s income to the community. This resources the langar (community kitchen), the gurdwara and charitable work. Khalsa Aid, founded in Britain, embodies dasvandh in practice by providing humanitarian aid globally without regard for race, religion or background. The Sikh principle of vand chhakna — sharing what one has with others — sits alongside dasvandh as an expression of the teaching that wealth is given by God and must be shared.

The Role of Charity and UK Organisations

Religious organisations have founded some of the most prominent international development charities operating in Britain and globally. Christian Aid, founded in 1945, works in over 30 countries addressing poverty and injustice; it draws on the Christian principle of loving your neighbour globally, citing Luke 10:25–37 (the Good Samaritan parable). Islamic Relief, founded in Birmingham in 1984, channels zakat and sadaqah from British Muslim communities to emergency relief and long-term development worldwide. World Jewish Relief, which traces its origins to 1933 when it helped Jews fleeing Nazi Germany, now works with vulnerable communities across the world. Khalsa Aid, founded in Britain in 1999, channels Sikh sewa and dasvandh into disaster relief and refugee support globally.

Religious traditions also raise questions about the nature of charity itself. Jewish tzedakah teaches that the highest form of giving enables independence rather than dependence. Buddhist teaching questions whether charity that does not address the structural causes of poverty is sufficient. Catholic Social Teaching distinguishes between immediate relief work and structural justice — the need to change the conditions that cause poverty, not merely to address its effects. This debate — between charitable giving as relief versus advocacy for structural change — is itself grounded in religious teaching and is a productive area for 12-mark evaluation questions.

Key Fact

Christian Aid (Christian — love your neighbour, Luke 10); Islamic Relief (Muslim — zakat and sadaqah, founded Birmingham 1984); World Jewish Relief (Jewish — tzedakah, origins 1933); Khalsa Aid (Sikh — sewa and dasvandh, founded Britain 1999). Each organisation translates its tradition’s teaching on wealth and poverty into direct action.
exam_tip_html:
For the 6-mark Explain question on wealth and poverty, you must name a source of religious teaching. Strong options: Genesis 1:28 and Acts 2:44–45 (Christian stewardship and sharing); Quran 2:110 on zakat; Deuteronomy 24:14–15 on fair wages; Leviticus 25 on the Jubilee. Name the source AND develop it: explain why the teaching leads believers to act in a particular way. A named charity (Christian Aid, Islamic Relief) can support your answer but does not replace a named source of scripture or teaching.

For the 12-mark Evaluate, a common statement is: “Religious people have a duty to give their wealth to those in need.” Arguments for should draw on zakat, tzedakah, dasvandh, stewardship, Acts 2, Deuteronomy 24. Arguments against should note that religions also affirm the legitimacy of wealth, the right to private property (Catholic Social Teaching), and the responsibility of individuals to work to support themselves. Non-religious perspectives (e.g. secular welfare-state arguments) should also be included. Your conclusion must say which side is stronger and WHY — and must be present, not implied.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Religious traditions do not condemn wealth outright but teach responsibilities: Christian stewardship (Genesis 1:28; Acts 2:44–45); Islamic zakat (2.5% obligatory giving, Quran 2:110); Jewish tzedakah (justice, not merely charity); Sikh dasvandh (one tenth to the community); Buddhist non-attachment (avoiding greed as one of the Three Poisons).
  • Exploitation is condemned across traditions — unfair pay (Deuteronomy 24:14–15; Rerum Novarum), excessive interest — riba in Islam (Quran 2:275) with debate about modern application — and people-trafficking. Each tradition grounds its opposition in the equal dignity of all persons.
  • UK religious charities — Christian Aid, Islamic Relief, World Jewish Relief, Khalsa Aid — translate their traditions' teachings on wealth and poverty into active work. The debate between immediate relief and structural justice is itself grounded in religious teaching.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct definition of 'zakat' in Islam?
A) The voluntary fasting during Ramadan
B) The obligatory annual giving of a portion of savings to those in need, one of the Five Pillars
C) The pilgrimage to Mecca undertaken once in a lifetime
D) The declaration of faith: 'There is no god but Allah'
practice_questions.marks: B) The obligatory annual giving of a portion of savings to those in need, one of the Five Pillars [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Sikh practice of tithing one tenth of one's income for the benefit of the community.
Explain two contrasting religious beliefs about the right attitude to wealth.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Two contrasting beliefs, each developed:
1 mark for a belief stated; 1 additional mark for development with reference to a specific tradition.
Acceptable examples:
- Christian stewardship teaches that wealth belongs ultimately to God; humans are caretakers responsible for using it wisely and sharing with those in need (Genesis 1:28) (1+1).
- Buddhist non-attachment teaches that clinging to wealth is greed (lobha), one of the Three Poisons causing suffering; wealth should be held lightly and shared through dana (1+1).
- Islamic teaching allows the lawful acquisition of wealth but requires zakat (2.5% giving) as a purification and redistribution; wealth concentrated without zakat is condemned (1+1).
- Sikh dasvandh requires giving one tenth of income to the community; the principle of kirat karna insists wealth must be earned honestly (1+1).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why religious believers oppose the charging of excessive interest on loans.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two well-developed reasons, each grounded in a specific religious tradition. At least one named source (e.g. Quran 2:275 on riba; Leviticus 25 on the Jubilee and debt cancellation; Deuteronomy 24 on fair treatment of the poor; Catholic Social Teaching). Both reasons clearly developed, explaining why the teaching leads to opposition to excessive interest. Sub-tradition or tradition named.
Secure (3-4): Two reasons present; one with a named source; development present but partial.
Developing (2): One reason developed, or two stated without development; source missing.
Emerging (1): Basic point; little religious knowledge; no source.

practice_questions.text:
'Religious people have a duty to give their wealth to those in need.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to religious teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Islamic zakat is obligatory, not optional: every Muslim above the nisab threshold must give 2.5% of savings annually (Quran 2:110).
- Jewish tzedakah is a duty grounded in justice (tzedek), not optional generosity: the poor have a right to receive, and the wealthy have an obligation to give.
- Acts 2:44-45 describes the early Christian community selling possessions and sharing with all who had need.
- Sikh dasvandh requires one tenth of income for the community; langar demonstrates this in practice at every gurdwara.
- Buddhist dana (generosity) is the first of the Six Perfections and is required for progress on the path.
Arguments against:
- Catholic Social Teaching affirms the right to private property (Rerum Novarum); the duty to give does not eliminate the right to keep some of one's earnings.
- Christian teaching distinguishes between obligatory giving (tithing, in some traditions) and voluntary charity; Jesus commended a spirit of generosity, not a legal demand.
- Religious traditions also teach that individuals have a responsibility to work to support themselves; the Sikh principle of kirat karna (honest work) emphasises self-reliance.
- Non-religious perspectives: secular welfare-state arguments hold that redistribution through taxation is more efficient and just than voluntary religious giving.
Non-religious perspectives: Humanists UK would argue for structural poverty reduction through policy, not only individual giving.
Mastering (10-12): Balanced argument on both sides; named religious teachings; at least one non-religious view; reasoned justified conclusion with clear reason why one side is stronger.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; some religious teaching; conclusion present but weakly justified.
Developing (4-6): One-sided or both sides undeveloped; generic religious knowledge; conclusion attempted.
Emerging (1-3): Basic points; little religious knowledge; no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Fatima volunteers with Islamic Relief in Birmingham. Give two ways in which Islamic teaching motivates her charitable work.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each valid way, up to 2 marks:
- The duty of zakat requires giving 2.5% of savings above the nisab threshold to those in need; Fatima may channel her zakat through Islamic Relief.
- The principle of sadaqah (voluntary charitable giving) encourages Muslims to give beyond zakat freely and without expectation of return.
- The concept of the ummah (worldwide community of believers) grounds the duty to support all Muslims in need, regardless of national origin.
- The Quranic teaching that all people have dignity conferred by Allah motivates working for the poor and vulnerable.

The teaching that wealth should always be given away
The principle that Christians should invest in ethical businesses

Charging interest or usury on loans, forbidden because it exploits borrowers and concentrates wealth unjustly
The pilgrimage tax paid by Muslims travelling to Mecca
The portion of zakat given directly to mosques

Sikh — sewa and dasvandh, founded in Britain 1999
